title: Basics of German Language
summary: German alphabet, pronunciation rules, greetings, farewells, basic phrases, and self-introduction.

grammar_rules.explanation: Long sound if followed by 1 consonant or 'H'. Short sound if followed by 2 consonants.
'ei' sounds like 'eye'. 'ie' sounds like 'ee'. 'eu/äu' sounds like 'oy'.
'w'=English 'v'. 'v'=English 'f'. 'st/sp' at start='sht/shp'. 'z'='ts'.
At start/middle: S sounds like Z. At end or doubled: S sounds like English S.
grammar_rules.formula: S start/middle = Z | S end/doubled = S

grammar_rules.explanation: Ä = 'ay' in 'may'. Ö = 'er' with rounded lips. Ü = 'ue' with rounded lips.

turns.speaker: A
turns.german: Hallo, ich heiße Thomas. Wie heißt du?
turns.english: Hello, my name is Thomas. What's your name?

turns.speaker: B
turns.german: Hallo, ich bin Julia. Ich komme aus Deutschland.
turns.english: Hello, I am Julia. I come from Germany.

turns.speaker: A
turns.german: Ich komme aus England. Ich wohne in Berlin.
turns.english: I come from England. I live in Berlin.

turns.speaker: B
turns.english: I am a student (f). And you?

title: Articles & Nouns
summary: Definite and indefinite articles, noun gender rules by suffix, compound nouns, days and months.

grammar_rules.explanation: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neutral), die (plural).
ein (masculine/neutral), eine (feminine). No indefinite plural.
Endings: -ig, -ling, -or, -ismus. Categories: Days, Months, Seasons, Directions.
Endings: -ung, -heit, -keit, -tät, -ion, -ik, -ie, -e (mostly). Numbers are feminine.
Endings: -chen, -lein, -ment, -um. Colors and metals are neutral.
The article comes from the LAST word in the compound.
examples: das Wasser + die Flasche = die Wasserflasche
der Fuß + der Ball = der Fußball

title: Pronouns, Numbers & Dates
summary: Personal pronouns, singular vs plural nouns, numbers 0-1M, phone numbers, ordinal numbers, dates.

grammar_rules.explanation: Read backwards: Unit + und + Ten.
1-19: add '-te'. 20+: add '-ste'. Exceptions: erste (1st), dritte (3rd), siebte (7th).
Masculine often adds '-e'. Feminine often adds '-en'. Neutral often adds '-er'. Words ending in -er/-el often only change article.

title: Sentence Structure & Time
summary: Basic sentence structure, verb position (Position 2 rule), present tense conjugation, sein/haben, negation, telling time, ordering and paying.

grammar_rules.explanation: The conjugated verb MUST always be in Position 2. Position means phrase, not word. Subject is usually Pos 1 or 3.
In a main clause (Hauptsatz), the Subject comes directly BEFORE or AFTER the verb.
'kein' negates indefinite nouns (replaces ein). 'nicht' negates verbs, adjectives, and definite nouns.
'Halb' + NEXT hour (8:30 = halb neun). Use 'vor' (to) and 'nach' (past).
Remove -en from infinitive to get stem. Add endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
examples: spielen: ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie spielen

grammar_rules.explanation: In present tense, only 2nd and 3rd person singular change stem. Changes: e→i, e→ie, a→ä.
grammar_rules.formula: Only du/er change: e→i | e→ie | a→ä

turns.speaker: A
turns.english: I would like to order please.

turns.speaker: B
turns.english: What would you like to drink?

turns.speaker: A
turns.english: I would like to pay please.

title: Questions & Time Prepositions
summary: Yes/No questions, W-questions, time prepositions (am/um/im), weather vocabulary, seasons, extended introduction.

grammar_rules.explanation: Verb comes FIRST (Position 1). Subject follows.
examples: Lernst du Deutsch? (Are you learning German?)

grammar_rules.explanation: W-word (Pos 1) + Verb (Pos 2) + Subject.
'um' for exact time, 'am' for days/dates, 'im' for months/seasons.

turns.english: I speak French, English and a little German.

turns.english: Today it is sunny and warm.

title: Adjectives & Colors
summary: Adjective usage, adjective endings in Nominative (definite, indefinite, no article), colors.

grammar_rules.explanation: After sein/werden, adjectives have NO ending.
After der/die/das: always add -e. Plural: add -en.
ein (masc) → -er. ein (neut) → -es. eine (fem) → -e.

turns.english: Do you like the red car?

turns.speaker: B

title: Modal & Separable Verbs
summary: Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, sollen, dürfen, mögen), separable verbs, daily routines.

grammar_rules.explanation: Conjugated modal verb at Position 2. Main verb (infinitive) goes to the END.
Prefix splits off and goes to the END in simple sentences. With modal verb: stays joined as infinitive at end.
examples: Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf (prefix at end)
Ich muss um 7 Uhr aufstehen (joined with modal)
grammar_rules.formula: Simple: prefix to END | With modal: joined infinitive at END

grammar_rules.explanation: Prefixes: ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, zurück-, statt-, fern-.

turns.speaker: A
turns.english: When do you have to get up tomorrow?

turns.speaker: B
turns.english: I want to get up at 8.

turns.speaker: B
turns.german: Ja, ich kaufe nach der Arbeit ein.

title: Past Tense (Präteritum)
summary: Simple past of haben and sein, regular/irregular Präteritum, transportation vocabulary, apologizing.

grammar_rules.explanation: Irregular but vital. Used in everyday speech (not just writing).
grammar_rules.formula: ich war | du warst | er war | wir waren | ihr wart | sie waren

grammar_rules.explanation: Also commonly used in speech.
grammar_rules.formula: ich hatte | du hattest | er hatte | wir hatten | ihr hattet | sie hatten

grammar_rules.explanation: Stem + -te + personal ending.
examples: machen → ich machte, du machtest, er machte

turns.speaker: B
turns.german: Ich war in Berlin. Ich hatte einen Termin.
turns.english: I was in Berlin. I had an appointment.

title: Perfect Tense & Housing
summary: Perfekt construction, Partizip II formation (regular/irregular/separable), haben vs sein, apartment and housing vocabulary.

grammar_rules.explanation: Helper verb (haben/sein) at Position 2 + Partizip II at END.
ge- + verb stem + -t. If stem ends in -t/-d, add -et. Verbs ending in -ieren: no ge-.
grammar_rules.formula: ge + stem + t | ge + stem(t/d) + et | -ieren → stem + t

grammar_rules.explanation: ge- + changed stem + -en. No fixed rule — must memorize.
ge- goes between prefix and base. Prefix + ge + base Partizip.
Use sein for movement (fahren, gehen, fliegen) or state change (aufstehen, sterben). Use haben for everything else.
examples: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren (sein - movement)
Ich habe Deutsch gelernt (haben - no movement)
grammar_rules.formula: sein = movement/state change | haben = everything else

title: Accusative Case & Professions
summary: Accusative articles, accusative pronouns, adjective endings in accusative, negation with keinen, professions.

grammar_rules.explanation: ONLY masculine changes. der→den, ein→einen, kein→keinen. Feminine/Neutral/Plural stay the same.
Subject (Nominativ) = WHO does action. Object (Akkusativ) = WHAT receives action.
examples: Der Hund sieht die Katze (Hund=subject, Katze=object)
grammar_rules.formula: Who verb? = Subject | What gets verbed? = Object

grammar_rules.explanation: After the verb 'sein', always use Nominativ (not Akkusativ).
examples: Das ist ein guter Mann (NOT: einen guten Mann)

grammar_rules.explanation: Same as Nominativ EXCEPT masculine: definite→-en, indefinite→-en.
examples: Ich sehe die schöne Frau (-e, no change)
grammar_rules.formula: Masculine Akk: always -en | Rest: same as Nom

turns.english: I am looking for a job.

turns.speaker: A
turns.german: Nein, ich rufe ihn gleich an.
turns.english: No, I'll call him right away.

title: Possessive Articles & Clothing
summary: Possessive articles (mein, dein, sein...) in Nominative and Accusative, clothing vocabulary.

grammar_rules.explanation: Possessives follow the same endings as 'ein'. Accusative masculine: add -en.
examples: Nominativ: mein Hund, meine Katze, mein Buch
Akkusativ: meinen Hund, meine Katze, mein Buch

turns.speaker: B

turns.english: No, that is not my sweater.

turns.speaker: B

title: Dative Case & Directions
summary: Dative articles, dative pronouns, dative verbs, location vs direction (Wo/Wohin), two-way prepositions, giving directions.

grammar_rules.explanation: der/das → dem. die → der. Plural die → den (+n on noun).
grammar_rules.formula: m/n: der/das→dem | f: die→der | pl: die→den(+n)

grammar_rules.explanation: ein(m/n) → einem. eine(f) → einer.
Static location (Wo?) = Dative. Movement/direction (Wohin?) = Accusative. Two-way prepositions take either depending on meaning.
examples: Wo bist du? Im Park (Dative - location)
Wohin gehst du? In den Park (Accusative - direction)

grammar_rules.explanation: Some verbs always take Dative object: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken, antworten, gratulieren.
grammar_rules.formula: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken, antworten, gratulieren → Dativ

grammar_rules.explanation: The preposition 'zu' always takes Dative.

title: Comparisons & Shopping
summary: Comparative and superlative forms, demonstrative pronouns (dieser/diese/dieses), grocery shopping vocabulary, frequency adverbs.

grammar_rules.explanation: Adjective + -er + 'als'. Many common adjectives get umlaut (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü).
'am' + adjective + '-sten'. Adjectives ending in -t/-d/-s/-z add '-esten'.
'dieser/diese/dieses' = 'this (specific)'. Endings follow definite article pattern.

turns.speaker: A
turns.german: Er ist süßer als der andere.
turns.english: It is sweeter than the other one.

turns.speaker: B

turns.english: Yes, but it's also more expensive.

title: Imperative & Health
summary: Imperative mood (commands) for du/ihr/Sie, body parts, health vocabulary, doctor appointments.

grammar_rules.explanation: Conjugated verb + Sie. Same as question form but with exclamation.
Verb stem only (drop -st ending, no pronoun). Verbs with e→i keep the change. Verbs with a→ä lose the umlaut.
grammar_rules.formula: Verb stem (no -st, no du) | e→i stays | a→ä drops

grammar_rules.explanation: Same as normal ihr-conjugation, but without the pronoun.
Prefix still goes to the end, even in imperative.
